blocks.x: I consider myself a fairly eco-conscious person. I reduce, reuse, recycle; I take public transit; I avoid using AI for meme-making and learning celebrity heights. But composting never really took. I'd try to gather food scraps in a plastic countertop compost bin in my kitchen, but emptying and cleaning the receptacle every couple days was messy and smelly and I'd give up after a couple weeks. In 2025, however, New York City made composting the law of the land and I knew I needed to figure out a more sustainable solution.

Electric kitchen composters and food recyclers promise to turn your food scraps into dried grounds or usable compost in a matter of hours, eliminating the need to transport a dripping bag of rotting food goo through your apartment and around the block to where your building keeps the communal bin (just me?). Like magic, these machines can reduce the volume of your food waste by up to 90%, so you can go weeks or months without emptying them. The downside? Many of them are very expensive.

To find out whether these appliances are worth the hefty price tag, a few fellow BA editors and I put them to use in our own kitchens. Nearly a year later, I have to say, it's hard to imagine life without mine.

What I love: Many of the appliances folks refer to as electric composters are actually just dehydrators—they reduce the volume of your food waste by drying and grinding it down. Reencle's products, however, use living microbes to create real compost that's ready to be added to your garden.

I was nervous that the microbe thing would mean the Reencle Gravity would be complicated or messy to set up. Not so. Your device comes with a bag of compost starter, little rodent-feed-looking pellets of microorganisms derived from soy and cheese. You just empty the contents into your Reencle along with a small pouch of “compost booster,” add water, and close the lid. Give the machine at least 3 hours to get churning before you start adding your food.

From there, it's really a set-it-and-forget-it situation. While many food recyclers run on “cycles" like a dishwasher (you tell it when to start, and then you keep it closed and running until the cycle ends), Reencle's composters are always at work breaking down your scraps. This means you can open the lid to add food whenever you like. Once the bin starts to fill up—which took months in my two-person household—you scoop out the compost to the “minimum” line, leaving the bin about ⅓ full so that the microbes can continue doing their thing.

At nearly $700, the Gravity is undeniably expensive, but it's less than the internet-favorite Mill Food Recycler. Also, Reencle often runs discounts and has two smaller models for under $500 in its product line.

Longterm testing notes: I've been using the Reencle Gravity for nine months now, and I've literally only emptied it twice. Granted, my household is just my husband and me, and we eat a lot of takeout. Once a year you'll need to replace the appliance's charcoal filter to prevent odors.

What I'd leave: The front of a machine has a motion sensor that triggers the top to open, an action accompanied by a beep and an electric whirring sound. This sensor, it turns out, is fairly sensitive. My husband and I would trigger it by moving our dining chairs; my dog would trigger it by sniffing. After a few weeks, the beep-whir got to be pretty annoying, so I put a piece of painter's tape over the sensor and now stick to opening the lid via a button on top of the device.

Another slightly irritating quirk is that the top only stays open for 9 seconds. This is usually time enough to scrape what you need inside, but when you're clearing a lot of dishes from dinner or scooping compost out of the machine, it can feel really quick. I've taken to taping the lid open when it's time to empty it. (The Reencle doesn't like this—it beeps at me when I prop the lid open for too long.) Ultimately, neither of these design shortcomings outweigh the appliance's convenience.

What I love: I'm embarrassed to admit it, but until recently, I had never composted. Living in New York City before composting became mandatory in 2025 meant I’d have to save food scraps in the freezer for days until I could find time to drop them off. With my love of Trader Joe's frozen meals, I wasn't willing to sacrifice that space. Then I found the Mill. A trash-can-sized food-waste dehydrator and grinder, the Mill turns almost any solid food, from chicken bones to avocado pits, into a dry, loamy mix that looks like soil. Overnight, it heats and grinds discarded organics, reducing their volume by about 80%. After using it for the last year, I can confidently say that it's the first composting solution that fit into my life—a designation that earned it a 2025 Gear of the Year award.

It took me a couple of days to notice, but the Mill removed essentially all food waste-related odor. The smell of discarded food wafting through your kitchen completely disappears. Once it's gone, you almost forget it was ever an issue. The only way you'll get any scent now is to stick your nose directly into the bucket, and even then it's faintly sweet and earthy.

Because it dehydrates everything, it takes me and my boyfriend just over a month to fill it up, and what comes out is completely dry. Soggy compostable bags leaking on the way to the bin are a thing of the past. The overnight cycle, adjustable via the app, doesn't interfere with cooking, and it's quiet enough that you'll probably forget it's running. You also have the option to keep the lid unlocked during processing, so you can continue to feed it with scraps while it’s recycling them.

What I'd leave: There's no getting around the footprint. The Mill takes up as much floor space as a trash can, which matters if you're already giving up space to trash and recycling bins. The lid can’t lock in an open position, so you have to keep your foot on the pedal the entire time, and it can get tedious during a long cooking session. The interior capacity is also smaller than the exterior suggests, closer to half the height of the can, so on dinner party nights scraps can pile up. I’ve occasionally had to keep some scraps on my counter overnight, but by morning, there's plenty of room again.

Finally, the finished product isn't a 1:1 replacement for compost. It's too concentrated to use directly as soil, but you can mix it in as an enhancer, add composting enzymes to finish the process in your backyard, or dump it into a municipal compost bin.
